CHAPTER XXVII. THE SILENT FOUNTAIN

I turned and followed the spotted leopardess, catching but one glimpse
of her as she tore up the brow of the hill to the gate of the palace.
When I reached the entrance-hall, the princess was just throwing the
robe around her which she had left on the floor. The blood had ceased to
flow from her wounds, and had dried in the wind of her flight.

When she saw me, a flash of anger crossed her face, and she turned her
head aside. Then, with an attempted smile, she looked at me, and said,

“I have met with a small accident! Happening to hear that the cat-woman
was again in the city, I went down to send her away. But she had one of
her horrid creatures with her: it sprang upon me, and had its claws in
my neck before I could strike it!”

She gave a shiver, and I could not help pitying her, although I knew
she lied, for her wounds were real, and her face reminded me of how she
looked in the cave. My heart began to reproach me that I had let her
fight unaided, and I suppose I looked the compassion I felt.

“Child of folly!” she said, with another attempted smile, “--not crying,
surely!--Wait for me here; I am going into the black hall for a moment.
I want you to get me something for my scratches.”

But I followed her close. Out of my sight I feared her.

The instant the princess entered, I heard a buzzing sound as of many
low voices, and, one portion after another, the assembly began to be
shiftingly illuminated, as by a ray that went travelling from spot to
spot. Group after group would shine out for a space, then sink back into
the general vagueness, while another part of the vast company would grow
momently bright.

Some of the actions going on when thus illuminated, were not unknown to
me; I had been in them, or had looked on them, and so had the princess:
present with every one of them I now saw her. The skull-headed dancers
footed the grass in the forest-hall: there was the princess looking in
at the door! The fight went on in the Evil Wood: there was the princess
urging it! Yet I was close behind her all the time, she standing
motionless, her head sunk on her bosom. The confused murmur continued,
the confused commotion of colours and shapes; and still the ray went
shifting and showing. It settled at last on the hollow in the heath, and
there was the princess, walking up and down, and trying in vain to wrap
the vapour around her! Then first I was startled at what I saw: the old
librarian walked up to her, and stood for a moment regarding her; she
fell; her limbs forsook her and fled; her body vanished.

A wild shriek rang through the echoing place, and with the fall of her
eidolon, the princess herself, till then standing like a statue in front
of me, fell heavily, and lay still. I turned at once and went out: not
again would I seek to restore her! As I stood trembling beside the
cage, I knew that in the black ellipsoid I had been in the brain of the
princess!--I saw the tail of the leopardess quiver once.

While still endeavouring to compose myself, I heard the voice of the
princess beside me.

“Come now,” she said; “I will show you what I want you to do for me.”

She led the way into the court. I followed in dazed compliance.

The moon was near the zenith, and her present silver seemed brighter
than the gold of the absent sun. She brought me through the trees to the
tallest of them, the one in the centre. It was not quite like the rest,
for its branches, drawing their ends together at the top, made a clump
that looked from beneath like a fir-cone. The princess stood close under
it, gazing up, and said, as if talking to herself,

“On the summit of that tree grows a tiny blossom which would at once
heal my scratches! I might be a dove for a moment and fetch it, but I
see a little snake in the leaves whose bite would be worse to a dove
than the bite of a tiger to me!--How I hate that cat-woman!”

She turned to me quickly, saying with one of her sweetest smiles,

“Can you climb?”

The smile vanished with the brief question, and her face changed to a
look of sadness and suffering. I ought to have left her to suffer, but
the way she put her hand to her wounded neck went to my heart.

I considered the tree. All the way up to the branches, were projections
on the stem like the remnants on a palm of its fallen leaves.

“I can climb that tree,” I answered.

“Not with bare feet!” she returned.

In my haste to follow the leopardess disappearing, I had left my sandals
in my room.

“It is no matter,” I said; “I have long gone barefoot!”

Again I looked at the tree, and my eyes went wandering up the stem until
my sight lost itself in the branches. The moon shone like silvery
foam here and there on the rugged bole, and a little rush of wind went
through the top with a murmurous sound as of water falling softly into
water. I approached the tree to begin my ascent of it. The princess
stopped me.

“I cannot let you attempt it with your feet bare!” she insisted. “A fall
from the top would kill you!”

“So would a bite from the snake!” I answered--not believing, I confess,
that there was any snake.

“It would not hurt YOU!” she replied. “--Wait a moment.”

She tore from her garment the two wide borders that met in front, and
kneeling on one knee, made me put first my left foot, then my right on
the other, and bound them about with the thick embroidered strips.

“You have left the ends hanging, princess!” I said.

“I have nothing to cut them off with; but they are not long enough to
get entangled,” she replied.

I turned to the tree, and began to climb.

Now in Bulika the cold after sundown was not so great as in certain
other parts of the country--especially about the sexton’s cottage; yet
when I had climbed a little way, I began to feel very cold, grew still
colder as I ascended, and became coldest of all when I got among the
branches. Then I shivered, and seemed to have lost my hands and feet.

There was hardly any wind, and the branches did not sway in the
least, yet, as I approached the summit, I became aware of a peculiar
unsteadiness: every branch on which I placed foot or laid hold, seemed
on the point of giving way. When my head rose above the branches
near the top, and in the open moonlight I began to look about for the
blossom, that instant I found myself drenched from head to foot. The
next, as if plunged in a stormy water, I was flung about wildly, and
felt myself sinking. Tossed up and down, tossed this way and tossed that
way, rolled over and over, checked, rolled the other way and tossed up
again, I was sinking lower and lower. Gasping and gurgling and choking,
I fell at last upon a solid bottom.

“I told you so!” croaked a voice in my ear.

[Reference Original]: CHAPTER I. OUTSIDE

‘No room!--Full up!’

He banged the door in my face.

That was the final blow.

To have tramped about all day looking for work; to have begged even for a job which would give me money enough to buy a little food; and to have tramped and to have begged in vain,--that was bad. But, sick at heart, depressed in mind and in body, exhausted by hunger and fatigue, to have been compelled to pocket any little pride I might have left, and solicit, as the penniless, homeless tramp which indeed I was, a night’s lodging in the casual ward,--and to solicit it in vain!--that was worse. Much worse. About as bad as bad could be.

I stared, stupidly, at the door which had just been banged in my face. I could scarcely believe that the thing was possible. I had hardly expected to figure as a tramp; but, supposing it conceivable that I could become a tramp, that I should be refused admission to that abode of all ignominy, the tramp’s ward, was to have attained a depth of misery of which never even in nightmares I had dreamed.

As I stood wondering what I should do, a man slouched towards me out of the shadow of the wall.

‘Won’t ’e let yer in?’

‘He says it’s full.’

‘Says it’s full, does ’e? That’s the lay at Fulham,--they always says it’s full. They wants to keep the number down.’

I looked at the man askance. His head hung forward; his hands were in his trouser pockets; his clothes were rags; his tone was husky.

‘Do you mean that they say it’s full when it isn’t,--that they won’t let me in although there’s room?’

‘That’s it,--bloke’s a-kiddin’ yer.’

‘But, if there’s room, aren’t they bound to let me in?’

‘Course they are,--and, blimey, if I was you I’d make ’em. Blimey I would!’

He broke into a volley of execrations.

‘But what am I to do?’

‘Why, give ’em another rouser--let ’em know as you won’t be kidded!’
[Reference Rewrite]: “No room. Full up.”

The door slammed with the dull, decisive thud of bureaucratic finality.

I stood in the freezing drizzle of the Hammersmith night, calculating the precise rate at which a man’s core temperature drops when he has been walking for fourteen hours on a deficit of three thousand calories. To have scoured the grime-choked streets of London all day for labor was an expected hardship; to have stooped to petition a casual ward for a night on a plank bed was a tactical compromise. To be denied even that miserable sanctuary was merely a lesson in the unreliability of institutional safety nets.

As I mentally mapped the grim reality of my situation, a figure detached itself from the shadows of the brick wall.

“Won’t let you in, eh?”

I turned to assess the man. His shoulders were hunched against the damp, his hands buried deep in the pockets of ruined trousers. He was a veteran of the gutters, worn down to the sinew, reeking of wet wool and cheap gin.

“He claims it’s at capacity,” I replied, my voice steady despite the shivering that had begun to seize my chest.

The man offered a jagged, cynical grin. “That’s the standard deterrent at Fulham. They always say it’s full. Keeps the ledger clean and the workload light.”

I studied him. “You’re suggesting it’s a calculated falsehood? An administrative bluff to filter the weak?”

“I’m saying the bloke’s having a laugh at your expense. If there’s square footage, they’re legally bound to take you. If I were you, I’d ring the bell again and make him do his job.”

There was a certain dark logic to testing the defenses twice. I approached the heavy door and yanked the iron bell-pull. The door swung open almost immediately, revealing the same grizzled pauper who acted as gatekeeper. If he had been the Prime Minister himself, he could not have worn a heavier mantle of unearned authority.

“Here again?” he sneered. “What’s the tactical objective here? Think I’ve got nothing better to do than wait on the likes of you?”

[Reference Original]: CHAPTER II. INSIDE

I realised, and, so to speak, mentally photographed all the little details of the house in front of which I was standing with what almost amounted to a gleam of preternatural perception. An instant before, the world swam before my eyes. I saw nothing. Now I saw everything, with a clearness which, as it were, was shocking.

Above all, I saw the open window. I stared at it, conscious, as I did so, of a curious catching of the breath. It was so near to me; so very near. I had but to stretch out my hand to thrust it through the aperture. Once inside, my hand would at least be dry. How it rained out there! My scanty clothing was soaked; I was wet to the skin! I was shivering. And, each second, it seemed to rain still faster. My teeth were chattering. The damp was liquefying the very marrow in my bones.

And, inside that open window, it was, it must be, so warm, so dry!

There was not a soul in sight. Not a human being anywhere near. I listened; there was not a sound. I alone was at the mercy of the sodden night. Of all God’s creatures the only one unsheltered from the fountains of Heaven which He had opened. There was not one to see what I might do; not one to care. I need fear no spy.

An instant before, the torrential Victorian night had been a blur of freezing misery; now, my senses sharpened into jagged relief. The cold was a physical enemy, steadily liquefying the marrow in my bones and draining the last of my cellular energy. But the open window presented a tactical anomaly, and more importantly, a lifeline.

It was a ground-floor sash, thrown wide to the deluge. I had only to breach the perimeter to secure dry cover. There was no watch, no patrol, no sign of life in the immediate vicinity. Out here, I was at the mercy of the elements, another anonymous casualty waiting to be swept into the Thames. The tramp at the casual ward had surrendered his freedom to the constabulary in exchange for a warm cell. I preferred to maintain my operational independence.

Perhaps the villa was empty. Civilian carelessness was a luxury of the secure and the comfortable. I considered knocking to alert the occupants of their vulnerability, perhaps angling for a meager reward. But experience in a harder school had taught me the futility of relying on the gratitude of the comfortable classes. More likely, I would be turned over to the authorities as a vagrant. Better to appropriate the shelter and vanish before dawn.

I leaned over the low brick wall, testing the air. The thermal differential was immediate; warmth bled from the dark aperture. Moving with deliberate silence, I vaulted the barrier. The ground beneath my boots felt cemented and stable. I pressed myself against the exterior masonry, listening at the crevice. Complete silence. It defied logic that any homeowner would leave a ground-floor blind fully raised and the sash open in this weather, but the battlefield is largely dictated by the blunders of the enemy.

"Turn," the command came, sharp and devoid of warmth.

I pivoted, tracking the spotted leopardess as she surged upward, tearing across the brow of the hill toward the palace gates. My vision caught her only in fleeting glimpses—a blur of muscle and fur against the stone—before she vanished into the courtyard beyond.

Reaching the entrance hall, I found the Princess mid-motion, hastily wrapping a robe around her frame where it had pooled on the floor. The blood had already congealed on her skin, dried stiff by the chill of her frantic flight. Upon seeing me, a flash of irritation crossed her features, causing her to turn her head sharply away. Then, forcing a brittle smile, she faced me again.

"I have encountered a minor mishap!" she declared, her voice tight. "Hearing rumors that the Cat-Woman has returned to the city, I descended to expel her. But she brought one of her abominable creations along. It leapt upon me, driving its claws into my throat before I could strike!"

She shivered violently. I felt a surge of pity, though my intellect screamed that she was lying; the wounds were genuine, and the pallor of her face mirrored the terror I had witnessed in the cave. My conscience reproached me instantly for allowing her to fight alone, and my expression betrayed the compassion rising within me.

"Child of folly!" she snapped, the smile dissolving into something sharper. "--Are you weeping? Do not cry! Wait here. I am entering the Black Hall momentarily. Fetch me something for these scratches."

I moved to follow, keeping pace just behind her. Fear prickled at the base of my spine; I dreaded the moment she disappeared from my line of sight. The instant she crossed the threshold, the air filled with a low, vibrating hum, akin to thousands of whispers merging into a single drone. Simultaneously, the vast assembly began to shift, illuminated intermittently by rays of light that traveled erratically from spot to spot. Groups of figures would flare into visibility, glowing with unnatural intensity, only to sink back into the gloom as another section of the crowd ignited.

Some scenes played out before me that I recognized intimately—I had lived them, or watched them unfold, alongside the Princess. Now, witnessing them simultaneously, the illusion shattered.

In the Forest-Hall, the skull-headed dancers trod the grass. There, at the doorway, stood the Princess, observing! In the Evil Wood, the battle raged; there, she urged the combatants onward! Yet physically, she remained motionless beside me, her head bowed onto her breast, a statue carved from grief.

The chaotic murmur continued, a swirling confusion of colors and shapes, while the shifting light persisted. Finally, the beam settled on a hollow in the heath. There, the Princess paced anxiously, attempting in vain to wrap vapor around her form.

Then, the distortion occurred. The Old Librarian stepped forward, regarding her silently. She collapsed. Her limbs abandoned her, fleeing outward as her physical form dissolved into mist. A wild shriek tore through the echoing chamber. With the vanishing of her eidolon—the phantom projection—the Princess herself, who had stood rigid before me, crumpled heavily to the ground, lying still.

I turned immediately and exited. Never again would I attempt to restore her.

Standing trembling beside the cage, I realized with chilling clarity that within the black ellipsoid, I had occupied the Princess's own mind. I saw the tail of the leopardess twitch once, a final spasm of malice.

While struggling to regain my composure, the Princess's voice cut through the silence beside me. "Come now," she commanded, her tone regaining its edge. "I require your assistance."

She led me into the court. I followed in a state of dazed compliance. The moon hung near the zenith, its silver radiance appearing far brighter than the golden light of the absent sun. She guided me through the trees to the tallest specimen, the central sentinel. Its branches drew inward at the apex, forming a cluster that resembled a fir-cone viewed from below.

The Princess stood directly beneath it, gazing upward. "Upon the summit of that tree grows a tiny blossom capable of healing my scratches instantly," she murmured, addressing the canopy rather than me. "I could transform into a dove and retrieve it, but I perceive a small serpent coiled in the leaves. Its bite would prove far deadlier to a bird than a tiger's bite would be to me... How I detest that Cat-Woman!"

She spun to face me, her expression softening into one of her sweetest smiles. "Can you climb?"

The smile evaporated as quickly as it appeared, replaced by a mask of profound suffering. I should have allowed her pain to consume her, yet the gesture of her hand pressing against her wounded neck struck a chord in my heart. I assessed the tree. Projections jutted from the trunk like the remnants of fallen palm fronds, offering potential footholds.

"I can ascend that tree," I stated.

"Not with bare feet!" she retorted.

In my haste to pursue the leopardess, I had discarded my sandals in my quarters.

"It matters not," I replied. "I have long since gone barefoot."

My gaze drifted upward, following the rough bark until my vision blurred at the highest branches. Moonlight shimmered like silvery foam across the rugged bole, and a faint breeze rustled the treetop with a sound reminiscent of water trickling softly into a pool. I stepped forward to begin my ascent.

The Princess halted me. "I cannot permit you to attempt this with exposed feet!" she insisted. "A fall from such height would be fatal."

"So would a bite from the snake!" I countered, admitting privately that I doubted the existence of any serpent.

"It would not harm *you*!" she shot back. "--Wait."

She tore from her garment the two wide borders meeting at her waist. Kneeling on one knee, she instructed me to place my left foot, then my right, onto the fabric strips. She bound them tightly around my ankles with the thick embroidery.

"You have left the ends dangling, Princess!" I observed.

"I possess no means to trim them," she admitted. "However, they are too short to snag on the branches."

Turning to the tree, I began to climb.

In Bulika, the cold after sunset was less severe than in other regions—particularly near the sexton's cottage—but as I ascended, the temperature plummeted. After climbing a mere few meters, I felt a biting chill that intensified with every step, reaching its peak among the upper branches. Shivers racked my frame, and I felt as though I had lost sensation in my extremities entirely.

There was virtually no wind, and the branches remained perfectly still. Yet, as I neared the summit, a peculiar instability seized me. Every limb I touched or stepped upon seemed poised to snap under my weight.

When my head finally cleared the canopy, bathed in the open moonlight, searching for the blossom, I was suddenly drenched from crown to toe. The next instant, as if cast into a violent tempest, I was thrashed about wildly, feeling myself plunge downward. Tossed up and down, flung side to side, rolling over and over, checked and reversed, I sank deeper and deeper. Gasping, gurgling, choking on the thin air, I crashed finally onto a solid surface.

"I told you so!" a voice rasped in my ear.
